title: Right and Wrong Choices
keyIdea: A right choice is honest, fair and kind, and it thinks about how other people will feel. Tell the truth, even after an accident: hiding it or blaming someone else breaks trust. Ask before you use things that belong to someone else. Share so each person gets the same. The right thing is sometimes the harder thing, and it is still right.

kid: Before you choose, stop and think: how will the other person feel? If Tom wants a go with the ball, giving him a turn makes him smile. Keeping it all day makes him sad.
Tell the truth, even when you made a mistake. An accident is not naughty. If you hide it or say the cat did it, people find out and trust you less. If you tell, they can help you fix it.
Some things are yours, like your teddy and your lunch. Some things belong to someone else, like a friend's crayons. Ask first. A toy you find in the park is still someone's. Give it to a grown-up.
Fair means each person gets the same. Six strawberries for three children is two each. The right thing can be hard, like saying no to a friend. It is still right, and you feel good after.
adult: This topic sits in the primary Relationships Education guidance for England. It asks pupils to learn why honesty and truthfulness matter, to respect other people and their things, and to be fair in friendships. PSHE plans for Key Stage 1 add the difference between right and wrong, and how choices have consequences for us and for others.

Children of five to seven are building a conscience: a sense of right and wrong that works even when no adult is watching. Four skills carry it. Take the other person's view (how will Tom feel?). Own up after an accident. Respect property: a thing is not yours just because no one is there. See fair as equal shares. Praise the choice and the reason, not only the result.

Common mistakes at this age: judging an act by the size of the damage, not the intention, so ten cups broken by accident seem worse than one broken on purpose. Thinking a lie is fine if no one finds out. Believing finders keepers. Treating fair as whatever the finder or the oldest child wants. Be careful not to punish a child who owns up to an accident, or they learn to hide things.

In the lab your child picks kind or unkind choices and watches a face change. They play out telling the truth, hiding a broken cup and blaming the cat, while Mum's trust hearts rise or fall. Then they sort six things into ask first or mine to use, share six strawberries fairly, and take the harder right path three times.

familyTip: When something goes wrong at home, say thank you first when your child owns up, then fix it together. Ask: how do you think they felt? and what would be fair?

visual.caption: Right choice or wrong choice? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Tell the truth about a spill

lab.caption: Flagship lab: choose kindly and watch faces change, play out the truth about a broken cup, ask before you borrow, share fairly and take the harder right path.

practice.prompt: Mia spills juice on the sofa by accident. What is the right thing to do?
practice.hint: Which choice is honest and helps fix the spill?
practice.explain: Telling a grown-up is honest, and they can help clean it. Hiding it or blaming the dog is not honest.

practice.prompt: There are {a} children. To be fair, each child gets {b} grapes. How many grapes do we need?
practice.hint: Count {b} grapes for each child, then add them all up.
practice.explain: {a} children with {b} grapes each need {=a*b} grapes. Then each child has the same.

practice.prompt: Sam wants to use Ava's new pens. What should he do first?
choices: Take them while she is out
practice.hint: The pens belong to Ava. What do we do with things that are not ours?
practice.explain: The pens are Ava's, so Sam asks first. Taking even one without asking is not right.

practice.prompt: There are {=2*k} biscuits for 2 children. To be fair, how many biscuits does each child get?
practice.hint: Give one to each child, then one more to each, until the biscuits are all gone.
practice.explain: {=2*k} biscuits shared the same between 2 children is {k} each.

pool.prompt: You find a teddy on a bench in the park. No one is there. What should you do?
pool.hint: Does the teddy still belong to someone?
pool.explain: The teddy still belongs to someone. A grown-up can help find the owner.

pool.prompt: Leo broke a cup by accident and told his mum. How does his mum feel about him telling her?
pool.hint: Think about trust. Is it good to know the truth?
pool.explain: Mum is glad Leo told the truth. She can trust him, and they can fix it together.

pool.prompt: Ben is sitting on his own at playtime and looks sad. What is a kind choice?
pool.hint: How would you feel if you were on your own?
pool.explain: Asking Ben to play helps him feel wanted. Walking past or laughing makes him feel worse.

pool.prompt: Your friend says: let's take a sweet from the shop, no one will see. What do you do?
pool.hint: Is it right to take something without paying, even if no one sees?
pool.explain: Taking without paying is stealing, even when no one sees. The right thing is to say no.

pool.prompt: There are {=3*k} stickers for 3 friends. To be fair, how many stickers does each friend get?
pool.hint: Share them out one at a time: one for each friend, again and again.
pool.explain: {=3*k} stickers shared the same between 3 friends is {k} each.

pool.prompt: Jo broke a toy. She says her little brother did it. Why is that wrong?
choices: It is a lie and her brother gets told off
It is fine if no one finds out
pool.hint: Who gets in trouble, and is it true?
pool.explain: Blaming her brother is a lie, and he gets told off for something he did not do.

pool.prompt: Zara has {a} toy cars and Tom has none. How many should Zara give Tom so they each have {=a/2}?
pool.hint: Fair means the same. Give Tom one car at a time until both have the same.
pool.explain: Zara gives Tom {=a/2} cars. Then Zara has {=a/2} and Tom has {=a/2}, so it is fair.

pool.prompt: Which one is a right choice?
choices: Saying sorry when you hurt someone
pool.hint: Which one is honest, fair or kind?
pool.explain: Saying sorry is honest and kind. Grabbing and telling secrets are unfair and unkind.
